nodes.bodyText:
Hi,
I am the main developer of the OpenTURNS platform and I noted many wrong assessments in the description of OpenTURNS in your theory guide:

The Rosenblatt transformation is available for nearly 10 years (see here)
The bootstrap resampling method is available for more than 8 years (see here)
From its inception, OT has been designed to take into account dependence through copulas. In addition to the most standard copulas, it offers several mechanisms to combine or to define copulas (ComposedCopula, OrdinalSumCopula, SklarCopula, EmpiricalBernsteinCopula, ExtremeValueCopula, Mixture), most of them being available long before you wrote your guide. Note that SkarCopula allows to define a copula from any continuous joint distribution (eg. from multivariate mixtures of distributions). It is even possible to define your own copula in Python, thanks to the OpenTURNSPythonDistribution python class.
You wrongly assert that it is not possible to define a custom distribution in OT. It is the exact purpose of the OpenTURNSPythonDistribution python class, a 5 years old feature (see here). The minimal information needed is the definition of the joint CDF and the range of the (potentially multivariate) distribution, same as in chaospy.
It is of course possible to create a multivariate distribution from a set of univariate distributions and a copula in OT since the very first version of OT more than 11 years ago, see ComposedDistribution  here, but many more options are available (Mixture, ConditionalDistribution, BayesDistribution to name a few)
Variance reduction sampling methods are available in OT since more than 11 years, and DirectionalSampling, LHS (with randomized version), ImportanceSampling, QuasiMonteCarlo (with randomized version) were available at the time you started chaospy.
Two orthonormalization algorithms were available in OT to compute 3 terms relation coefficients at the time you started chaospy, see GramSchmidtAlgorithm and ChebychevAlgorithm, the first one being the modified version of the algorithm to improve its stability and the second one being based on modified moments. An adaptive version of the Stieltjes algorithm has been introduced at the end of 2015, allowing to build the 3 terms relation for orthonormal polynomials associated to any continuous or discrete univariate distribution (assuming they have finite moments of any order)
The UnivariatePolynomial class implements the full algebra of 1D polynomials as well as many other features for nearly 10 years
Spectral projection is available for more than 9 years using the IntegrationStrategy class
The collocation method (LeastSquaresStrategy) has always been available with all the sampling schemes for more than 10 years. There were 7 of them not counting variations (and not only 4) at the time you started chaospy
This report covers only the sections 1.1 and 1.2 of your guide. There are probably many more wrong assertions I will report soon.
You may have a look here to get some additional insights on isoprobabilistic transformation (title in French but content in English).
Regards
Régis LEBRUN

def calc_poly(poly, x):
    exp = 0.0

    for i, coeff in enumerate(poly):
        exp += (coeff*np.power(x, degree-i))
    return exp

def p1(x):
    return ( 1. + (1.4)**2./(0.75*x + 3.8)**2.0)**0.5

def p2(x):
